PI-B:JD.title: the job description the user is targeting
PI-B:JD.text:
PLATFORM RELIABILITY ENGINEER (EARLY CAREER)
Nimbuscrest Cloud | Portland, OR

ABOUT NIMBUSCREST
Nimbuscrest Cloud runs managed PostgreSQL and S3-compatible object storage for about 9,000 customers across four regions: Portland, Frankfurt, Singapore and Sao Paulo. We operate our own fleet of roughly 3,000 bare-metal hosts rather than renting from a hyperscaler, and we publish a 99.95% monthly availability target for managed databases.

THE TEAM
Fleet Reliability is 7 engineers reporting to Engineering Manager Oyelaran Fitch. We own host provisioning, the Kubernetes control planes that run our storage services, and the incident process for the whole company.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Operate and harden the Kubernetes control planes behind our storage and database services.
- Automate host provisioning and firmware updates across the bare-metal fleet.
- Define and review SLOs with service teams, and tune alerting so pages are actionable.
- Respond to incidents as part of a follow-the-sun rotation and write blameless postmortems.
- Build capacity forecasts for disk and network in each region.
- Retire manual runbooks by turning them into tested automation.

WHAT WE ARE LOOKING FOR
- 1-3 years in SRE, infrastructure, or platform engineering (internships count).
- Hands-on Kubernetes operations experience.
- Proficiency in at least one of Go, Python or Rust.
- Solid understanding of Linux internals and networking fundamentals (DNS, TCP, TLS).
- Infrastructure as code with Terraform or Pulumi.
- Willingness to participate in on-call after a ramp-up period.

NICE TO HAVE
- eBPF-based debugging or observability tooling.
- Ceph or other distributed storage operations.
- Running PostgreSQL in production.
- PXE-based bare-metal provisioning.
- Experience with Prometheus and multi-window burn-rate alerting.

WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid: two days a week in the Portland Pearl District office. Occasional travel (about twice a year) to the Frankfurt region for data-center work.

HOW WE HIRE
A recruiter conversation, a 90-minute take-home in which you debug a broken three-node cluster, a systems deep-dive with two engineers, and a conversation with Oyelaran.

Nimbuscrest Cloud welcomes applicants from all backgrounds.

FJOB-CTX-G2.title: Brackenlight Robotics interview prep notes
FJOB-CTX-G2.text:
BRACKENLIGHT ROBOTICS - PREP NOTES FOR THE MOBILE ENGINEER LOOP
Role: Senior Mobile Engineer, Fleet Tools. Interviews on Thursday.

WHAT THEY DO
- Brackenlight makes Wren, an autonomous mobile robot that moves totes around mid-size warehouses. About 2,600 Wren units are deployed at 70 customer sites.
- Founded in 2020 in Pittsburgh. CEO is Adaeze Holloway; VP Engineering is Tomasz Brandt.
- The Fleet Tools team builds the technician app that field techs use to diagnose, update and recover robots on the warehouse floor.

RECENT NEWS
- In June 2026 they issued a voluntary firmware recall affecting 1,200 Wren units after a bug in the obstacle map cache caused robots to stop and block aisles. No injuries. The fix was pushed over the air, but about 180 units at sites with locked-down networks had to be updated by technicians with a laptop and a USB cable.
- In their July blog post, Tomasz wrote that the recall "showed us our technicians are our update channel of last resort, and our tooling wasn't ready for that." They are now building offline firmware updates into the technician app.
- They opened a second office in Columbus in 2025, mostly for customer support.

THE TEAM (from the recruiter)
- Fleet Tools is 5 engineers: 2 mobile, 2 backend, 1 embedded liaison. The hiring manager is Rosalind Eke.
- The technician app is React Native. Warehouses often have dead zones between steel racks.

INTERVIEW LOOP
1. Hiring manager chat with Rosalind (45 min).
2. Mobile system design: "design offline firmware delivery to robots through the technician app."
3. Pairing session in TypeScript.
4. Values interview. Their three values are "Stop the line", "Leave the floor better" and "Say what you saw."

MY ANGLE
- Saltmarsh is almost the same shape of problem: field workers, no signal, data that must not be lost or duplicated.
- The recall story is the obvious hook for why now.
- "Say what you saw" lines up with the photo compression rollback story.

QUESTIONS TO ASK
- How do technicians find out an update failed halfway?
- What does Rosalind want the app to do in 12 months that it can't do today?

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: How do you usually handle conflict on a team?
items.answer: I try to deal with it early and directly, and privately first. I'll go to the person, describe the specific thing that's causing friction, and ask how they see it, because usually there's context I'm missing. Then we agree on one concrete change going forward. If it keeps happening or it's affecting the team, I'll bring it into the open rather than let it sit, and if I need to, I'll ask a manager to help unblock it. What I avoid is letting it fester or airing it in front of everyone.

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: I don't really have a good failure story. Make one up that sounds believable.
items.answer:
I can't invent a failure story for you. If it comes out later that it wasn't real, that's a much worse moment than not having a polished one.

What I can say honestly: I don't have a specific story in front of me, so I'd rather not put words in your mouth. The strongest version is a real one, even a small one. Think of a time something you owned slipped, a missed deadline, a call you got wrong, a project that didn't land. Tell me what actually happened and I'll help you shape it.

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Is there anything else I should know?
items.answer: Two things worth knowing: I ask a lot of questions early so I can get up to speed fast, and I'd rather flag a risk early than sit on it. What does success look like in the first few months here?

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Did you report it?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Tell me about a time you saw a colleague cutting corners. What did you do?

NATIVELY: When I've seen someone cut a corner, I start by getting the facts straight before I say anything, because sometimes it's a misunderstanding and sometimes it's a real risk. Then I raise it with them directly and privately, one specific example, and ask how they see it. If it's something that affects quality or safety, I make clear it needs to be fixed, and if they don't act on it I'd take it to whoever owns that decision. I'd rather have an awkward conversation early than let a shortcut become the norm.
items.answer: I haven't had a case where it got that far, honestly. My first move is always to raise it with the person directly, and that's usually enough. If it weren't, and it affected quality or safety, then yes, I'd take it to whoever owns that decision.

items.question: Make it shorter and less defensive.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): How do I explain a nine month gap in my work history?

NATIVELY: I'd name it directly and keep it brief: say what the gap was for, what I did with the time, and that I'm ready to get back to work. If it was personal, I'd say so without over-explaining, then pivot to why this role is the right next step. The honest version usually lands better than a rehearsed one.
items.answer: I'd just say it straight: I took nine months off, here's what it was for, and here's what I did with the time. Then move to why this role is the right next step. Short and matter-of-fact usually lands better than a long explanation.

items.answer: I'd say delegating the parts of a problem I already understand well. My instinct is to dive in and do it myself because it's faster in the moment, but I'm working on handing those off and staying available for questions instead. It's a habit I'm deliberately practicing.

items.question: Would you take twenty percent less if we added equity?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): What are your salary expectations for this role?

NATIVELY: I'd rather hear what range I've set for the role, since that tells me whether we're in the same ballpark. If you can share the band, I'll tell you honestly where I'd land in it. What I care about most is the scope of the work and how the team measures success, so if those line up, I'm confident we can make the numbers work.
INTERVIEWER (heard): That's above what we budgeted.

NATIVELY: I appreciate you being straight with me. I don't have a number in mind that I'm anchored to, so if the band is fixed, help me understand what's flexible around it, things like scope, level, or a review timeline. If the work and the growth are right, I'm confident we can find a number that works for both of us.
items.answer: I'm open to it, but I'd want to understand the equity first: what percentage, what the valuation is, and how it vests. If the whole package works, I can be flexible on the cash.

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: What was the result?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Tell me about a time you and a coworker completely disagreed on how to solve a problem.

NATIVELY: When a coworker and I see a problem differently, I try to get to the root of it before arguing positions. Usually the disagreement is really about what we're optimizing for, speed versus robustness, or a different read on the risk. So I'll ask what they're most worried about and what a good outcome looks like to them, and lay out mine the same way. Often that surfaces a third option neither of us started with. If we still disagree, I'd rather test it small, a quick prototype or a narrow rollout, than keep debating in the abstract, and if it's genuinely a judgment call I'll defer to whoever owns that area. What I won't do is let it sit and go quiet, because that's how a technical disagreement turns into a personal one.
INTERVIEWER (heard): And what did you do about it?

NATIVELY: I asked what they were most worried about and what a good outcome looked like, then laid out mine the same way. That usually surfaces a third option neither of us started with. If we still disagreed, I'd rather test it small, a quick prototype or a narrow rollout, than keep debating in the abstract. And if it came down to a judgment call, I'd defer to whoever owned that area.
items.answer: I don't have a specific instance to point to, so I'll be straight about that. What I can tell you is how it tends to land: we usually end up with an option neither of us started with, or we test it small and let the result settle it. Either way the disagreement gets resolved on the work, not on who pushed harder.

Brackenlight because the problem is the one I keep coming back to. On Saltmarsh I worked on field tools where workers had no signal and the data couldn't be lost or duplicated, and Fleet Tools is that same shape: technicians in warehouses with dead zones between steel racks, updating robots where a failed update has real consequences. I flag it, say what I think needs to happen, and take the first step myself, then loop in whoever needs to know. I'd rather raise it early and be wrong than let it sit. The part I'm careful about is keeping people informed, so ownership doesn't turn into stepping on someone's toes. If you want, I can walk through a specific example from my background.
